verses.1:
Al-Mizan explains that God swears by the wise Qur’an that the Prophet is truly among the messengers and is upon a mighty, clear, straight path leading its travellers to God, human happiness, perfected servitude, and nearness to Him. The Qur’an is ḥakīm because it contains profound truths and what proceeds from them: religious laws, signs and stories for reflection, and moral exhortations.

“[This is] a revelation from the Mighty, the Merciful” describes the Qur’an as revealed by God and marked by both grandeur and mercy. God’s might means that refusal to worship Him, and the lies of deniers, do not weaken or disgrace Him; His mercy remains expansive toward those who follow the reminder and fear Him unseen. He gains nothing from their faith, but sends messengers and reveals the Qur’an to guide them to happiness and perfection. Thus some incur punishment, while others are encompassed by His mercy.

The revelation and mission are meant to warn a people whose fathers had not been warned, and who therefore are heedless; mā in mā undhira abāʾuhum means “not.” Qawm may mean the Quraysh and those associated with them, with “their fathers” being their more recent forefathers, since earlier Arabs had received prophets; or it may mean all people of the Prophet’s time, since his mission was universal and a long period had passed since Jesus. This is the meaning that first appears from the verses.

verses.7:
Al-Mizan holds that the oath in laqad ḥaqq al-qawl means that most of them have merited the divine decree of punishment: they have become cases in which that decree is fulfilled. The “word” is this decree, as in God’s declaration to Iblīs that He will fill hell with him and his followers (38:84–85).

Following Iblīs means obeying the temptations and suggestions he implants in hearts; this leads to rebellion and arrogance toward the truth. Those who become wholly devoted to worldly life and turn from the hereafter have their hearts, ears, and eyes sealed, and consequently can no longer find the way back to faith. Thus the decree of punishment is fulfilled upon rejectors, who enter hell as arrogant people.

Accordingly, fa- in fa-hum lā yuʾminūn expresses the natural consequence of this condition, not a particular reason, as some exegetes have supposed.
verses.8: Al-Mizan explains that aʿnāq means “necks,” aghlāl are shackles that bind a person’s hands to the neck, and muqmaḥūn means those whose heads are raised. Their chains run from their chests to their chins, fixing their heads upward so that they cannot see or distinguish the path before them. The indefinite aghlāl conveys the chains’ immense and frightening character. The verse thus explains why they do not believe.
verses.9: Al-Mizan reads barriers before and behind as enclosure from every side and covering as preventing sight, explaining the preceding shackles. Tafsīr al-Rāzī illustrates two forms of blindness: shackles prevent inward self-seeing, while surrounding barriers prevent outward vision of the horizons and God’s signs; losing both destroys sight entirely. Al-Mizan itself concludes that their chained, raised heads and enclosure leave them unable to see or be guided: God deprives them of guidance because of ingratitude, deliberate unbelief, perversity, and rebellion. Such descriptions disclose a person’s hidden inward life, which material senses cannot see now but death and resurrection reveal; they have a real form and are not merely figures.
verses.10: Al-Mizan says that the verse most apparently explains and reinforces the preceding three verses: it summarizes their point and prepares for the statement that only those who follow the reminder can be effectively warned. It may instead be connected to “they do not see,” meaning that, because they do not see, warning and not warning them are alike and they will not believe.
verses.11:
Al-Mizan explains that innamā restricts effective warning to those who follow the reminder, namely the Qur’an: they believe in it, heed it, and incline toward it when it is recited. The past tenses of “follow” and “fear” indicate the certainty that one who fears God will follow the message.

To fear the Merciful unseen is to stand in awe of God before the veil is lifted at death and resurrection, not, as some exegetes farfetchedly maintain, merely to fear Him in private rather than hypocritically. Calling Him “the Merciful” shows that this fear is joined to hope. This is the servant’s ideal state: neither secure from God’s wrath nor despairing of His mercy.

The indefinite forms of forgiveness and generous reward emphasize immense forgiveness and an immeasurably generous reward—the garden. The Prophet is therefore to give these glad tidings to those whose hopeful fear of the unseen Merciful makes his warning effective.
verses.12:
Al-Mizan explains that giving life to the dead means resurrecting them for recompense. What they have sent forth is the deeds they performed in life and sent ahead into death; what they have left behind is the enduring legacy of those deeds. Such legacies may be good, such as beneficial knowledge or a mosque used for prayer, or evil, such as an enduring heretical practice. The alternative claim that the former means intentions and the latter consequences of deeds is somewhat remote from the verse’s apparent meaning.

The recording of what people sent forth and left behind is the work of angelic scribes in individuals’ scrolls of deeds. This is distinct from accounting for all things in the clear registry (imām mubīn), which is the protected tablet (al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ). The Qur’an affirms a book encompassing everything, books belonging to each nation, and each person’s individual book; the distinction is also indicated by the clear registry’s comprehensiveness, the individual books’ specificity, and the different verbs for writing and accounting.

The clear registry is the unalterable tablet containing the details of God’s decree for creation, and is also called the protected tablet (al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ), the mother book (umm al-kitāb), and the clear book (kitāb mubīn). Perhaps “clear registry” indicates that it contains both the firmly fixed decrees of creation and the scrolls of deeds. The view that it means people’s scrolls of deeds is unfounded; the view that it means God’s knowledge is likewise more or less unfounded, unless this means His active knowledge (ʿilmuhu al-fiʿlī).

Al-Mizan also rejects the claim that the protected tablet records events only until resurrection because, being physical, it could contain only finitely many things. Although a finite object cannot contain infinite things, restricting “all things” to the period before judgement is arbitrary and unfounded. The verse concludes the preceding contrast between those who have earned punishment and those who follow the reminder and fear their unseen Lord: all life belongs to God, and the deeds and legacies of both groups are preserved with Him, who knows what each will receive.
verses.13: Al-Mizan explains that a parable (mathal) is a story or statement intended to convey a point. The Prophet is commanded to relate the town’s story as a likeness for his hearers, who stand in the same situation, and it illustrates divine reward and punishment. Grammatically, mathalan is the second object of “set forth,” placed before “the people of the town” so that the intervening wording does not disrupt the sense.
verses.14: Al-Mizan explains that ʿazzaznā, “We strengthened,” is related to ʿazīz, meaning mighty or strong. The verse clarifies the time when messengers came to the town: God sent two messengers, the people denied them, and He reinforced them with a third. Together they declared that God had sent them.
verses.15:
Al-Mizan explains that the townspeople denied that a human being could receive revelation. Because they themselves were neither prophets nor recipients of revelation, they wrongly generalized their own condition to all human beings and concluded that God had sent no revelation.

Their use of “the Merciful” (al-Raḥmān) shows that, like other polytheists, they acknowledged God and His noble attributes, while holding that He had entrusted the governance of creation to beings near to Him, such as honored angels. They treated those beings as lords and gods, while viewing God as the Lord of Lords. Possibly, the name al-Raḥmān is used to draw attention to God’s forbearance and mercy before their rejection of manifest truth.

“You do nothing but lie” means that they charged the messengers with lying in their present claim to revelation, not that they alleged the messengers were inherently or continually liars.
verses.16:
Al-Mizan notes that the passage does not recount the messengers’ answer to the objection that they were merely human, since analogous Qur’anic accounts have already given that answer. Instead, they affirm that their Lord knows they were sent and that their sole duty is clear delivery of the message.

“Our Lord knows” functions as an oath, while innā and la- in innā ilaykum la-mursalūn intensify their assertion. Their concern is neither to gain belief, payment, reward, nor personal benefit, but to convey the message plainly and establish conclusive proof. Balāgh means tablīgh, the delivery or spreading of the message.

verses.18: Al-Mizan explains that the townspeople address the messengers. Taṭṭayyur means regarding something as inauspicious or taking it as an evil omen. They deem the messengers an ill omen and threaten that, unless they cease proclaiming their message, they will stone or burn them and inflict severe, painful torment on them.
verses.19:
Al-Mizan explains that the messengers answer the townspeople by saying that the real evil omen is with the townspeople themselves: by rejecting divine unity and turning to polytheism, they face the ominous consequence. Although some exegetes understand ṭāʾirukum as a person’s fortune, good or bad, arising from his deeds, the following rebuke better supports the sense of an evil portent.

“What if you were reminded?” rebukes them for meeting a reminder of the truth—God’s oneness and the return to Him—with obstinacy, threats, and omens. Its unstated consequence is left unspoken because expressing it would be inappropriate. Their persistent refusal stems from their being a prodigal people, habitually exceeding the limits in disobedience to God.
verses.20:
Al-Mizan explains that aqṣā al-madīna means the outer edge of the city. The shift from qarya to madīna indicates the city’s size and the effort required for the man to rush from its outskirts. Unlike the wording of (28:20), the precedence of “from the outskirts of the city” here perhaps emphasizes that the man and the messengers could not have colluded in their message.

Arguments over the man’s name, lineage, and occupation are irrelevant to the verse. What matters is his faith-filled support of the messengers: he sincerely worshipped God because God is worthy of worship, rather than from desire for Heaven or fear of Hell. He confronted his people’s rationale for worshipping demigods, established that God alone should be worshipped and that the messengers spoke the truth, and believed in them. For this, he was among the honored.
verses.21:
Al-Mizan explains that “Follow those who do not ask you for anything, and they are guided” further identifies the messengers whom the people must follow. One must not follow a person who is misguided; nor should one heed even a truth-speaker whose aim is corrupt, such as seeking wealth or rank. But one who speaks truth and seeks no such gain must be followed.

The messengers meet both conditions: God has guided them to call to His oneness, and they seek no wealth or position from their people. Their proof for divine unity begins with “Why should I not serve the One who created me?” (36:22), while “Our Lord knows that we were sent to you as messengers” (36:16) confirms that they ask no return for their mission.
verses.22:
Al-Mizan presents these verses as a proof of God’s oneness and a refutation of other gods. Although the speaker appears to speak about himself, “and to whom you shall return” addresses his people and appeals to their shared human condition and fiṭra. Every human being has been created by God; because He brought the human being into being and truly owns his person, attributes, and acts, the human being must worship Him alone, because He is worthy of worship. The reminder of their return to Him warns them of reckoning and just recompense. While worship and faith belong to God alone, most people worship from fear, hope, or both rather than at this level of sincerity.

The polytheists argued that God’s essence lies beyond sensory, imaginative, and intellectual perception, and thus worshipped angels, jinn, or human saints as near beings who might intercede to obtain good and avert harm. Al-Mizan replies first that, even if His essence cannot be intellectually comprehended, God is known through attributes unique to Him, above all His giving all things being and creating them from nothing; refusing to approach Him through these attributes is obstinacy. Second, any intercession these beings possess is itself granted and limited by God’s will and permission: “None can intercede without His permission” (10:3). When God firmly wills harm, they cannot alter His decree, bring good, or repel misfortune.

Calling God “the Merciful” (al-Raḥmān) indicates the vastness of His mercy and that every blessing proceeds from Him. Since both good and ill and the cosmic order are administered by Him—even where angels convey aspects of His mercy—lordship and divinity truly belong to Him alone.

verses.24: Taking gods besides God would therefore be clear error.
verses.25:
Al-Mizan takes the man to be speaking to the messengers. “Hear me” means “bear witness,” and “I believe in your Lord” reaffirms his faith after he has argued for the truth. He asks the messengers to witness his belief and thereby supports them before the listening people.

Some exegetes take him to address the people, either challenging them to heed him and believe, declaring indifference to what they may do to him, or seeking to divert their attack from the messengers. Al-Mizan rejects this as problematic: he calls God “your Lord,” whereas the people regarded their demigods as lords. The proposed restriction—“your Lord who has established proof of His lordship for you”—has no indication in the text.
verses.26:
Al-Mizan holds that “Enter the garden” indicates that the man was killed by his people, after which a heavenly voice immediately commanded him to enter it. The succeeding account of the people’s destruction supports this reading: his killing led directly to the garden. This garden is the garden of barzakh, the intermediary realm, rather than the eternal Paradise after resurrection.

The view that it means entry into eternal Paradise on the Day of Resurrection, expressed in the past tense for certainty, has no evidence. Likewise unfounded is the claim that God raised him bodily to heaven to remain there until the Final Hour. The suggestion that the townspeople mockingly told him “Enter the garden” while killing him does not fit his subsequent wish that they knew what he found after receiving that command.

His words continue his counsel to his people after death: he wishes they knew how his Lord forgave and honored him. Absolute designation as mukramīn, “the honored ones,” belongs only to honored angels and to believers of complete faith, whether the sincere (mukhliṣīn) or those made sincere and purified (mukhlaṣīn). The verse is therefore among the proofs for barzakh.

verses.28: Al-Mizan explains that “after him” means after the man was killed. The first min marks the point of departure, while the second intensifies the negation. Divine vengeance had been decreed for his people, yet God required no heavenly host or preparation to destroy them; He did not send such hosts against them or the ancient peoples. A single cry eradicated them.
verses.29: Al-Mizan explains that their destruction came solely through the divine will: it was only a single cry. Its indefiniteness and description as single portray it as a lone, insignificant thing. The separate verse answers the implied question of what destroyed them. They were suddenly left still, unable to hear or sense, and became dead and motionless.
verses.30:
Al-Mizan explains that the vocative “Alas for [My] servants!” conveys an especially emphatic regret, whose cause is that whenever a messenger comes to people, they mock him. “Servants” means human beings generally; their rejection is especially grievous because they are God’s servants rebelling against their Master’s call, not merely rejecting sincere advice.

The words are God’s, not the man’s final speech. Al-Mizan consequently rejects interpretations that make “servants” the messengers, angels, or both, or that make the man the one expressing regret.
verses.31: Al-Mizan explains that the verse rebukes those for whom woe was declared. Qurūn is the plural of qarn, the people of a single era, so “how many generations” emphasizes people after people. The destroyed generations cannot return to the servants addressed in the verse—that is, they cannot return to their former ease and luxury after divine punishment. The living are therefore reproached for failing to take heed of the many past peoples God obliterated.
verses.32: Al-Mizan explains that the construction stresses an exceptionless gathering: all of them will be gathered together before God. They shall be brought before Him on the Day of Resurrection for reckoning and recompense.
verses.33: Al-Mizan presents the revival of dead earth as a sign of God’s lordship and His care for human sustenance. The sign is more precisely the barren earth itself, upon which life appears as grain and other edible produce. God causes grain-bearing plants to sprout, and “from it” means from that grain people eat; thus the verse displays the fulfillment of the divine provision of sustenance.
verses.34: Al-Mizan explains that jannāt are densely treed orchards, nakhīl means palm trees, and aʿnāb denotes grapevines and their fruit. Springs are called ʿuyūn because they resemble something split open, and fajjarnā describes the earth opening so that water bursts forth.
verses.35:
Al-Mizan explains that the l- in li-yaʾkulū marks the result of creating gardens and causing springs to flow: people eat their fruits. The pronoun in thamarihi may refer to the placing of the gardens, or to what has been described, functioning demonstratively; proposed references exclusively to palms, spring water, gushing forth, or God are baseless.

The commentary takes mā in wa mā ʿamilat aydīhim as negation: human hands did not create these fruits and therefore have no share in administering sustenance. Although some read mā as “what,” so that people eat what their hands make from fruits, or as a relative pronoun meaning “what their hands have wrought,” Al-Mizan rejects both. The verses are demonstrating God’s exclusive lordship through His management of creation, and ending with human effort would introduce an implication of partnership; were human capacity intended, it would have been expressly attributed to God’s gift.

The question about gratitude rebukes their thanklessness. They should acknowledge God’s lordship and divinity through verbal thanks and worshipful acts. Al-Rāghib’s distinction is that ʿamila ordinarily denotes intentional, goal-directed action and can be connected to good or evil, unlike faʿala.
verses.36:
Al-Mizan holds that the verse glorifies God as free of defect and need while proclaiming the vastness of His creation. He created all things in pairs or coupled forms—such as active and passive, male and female, or positive and negative—including plants, animals, and human beings; mating pairs require one another to produce a third, whereas God is above such dependence.

“What the earth grows” primarily means plant pairs and likely also includes animal life; “their own selves” means human beings; and “what they know not” covers things wholly or partly unknown to them, including unknown modes of procreation. The exclamation is glorification, not merely information. Al-Mizan rejects interpreting azwāj as merely types, subtypes, genera, or species, since zawj signifies compatible, coupled things. Citing Al-Rāghib, it notes that zawj includes male and female animals and any coupled pair, whether alike, opposite, or compound; each half requires its counterpart to attain its proper function.
verses.37: Al-Mizan treats the sudden disappearance of daylight and onset of darkness as a sign of God’s lordship and continuous management of human life. Although naslakhu usually means to extract or strip and normally takes ʿan, here it means taking away and therefore takes min. The description accords with the Qur’anic presentation of night and day entering one another: darkness surrounds people at nightfall, daybreak penetrates it with light, and when daylight vanishes night again envelops what had been illuminated. The expression may also be understood figuratively or metaphorically.
verses.38:
Al-Mizan explains tajrī as movement toward a place. Li-mustaqarrin lahā can mean that the sun moves toward or until its resting place, whether its final end, the time of sunset, or its descent below the horizon. Though it appears from the earth to circle it, the commentary states that scientific research finds the sun travels toward Vega.

The sun continues moving while the present order of the world endures; when it comes to rest, this world ends. This accords with an alternate reading attributed to Ahl al-Bayt and others: and the sun runs, with no rest [wa al-shams tajrī lā mustaqarra lahā instead of wa al-shams tajrī li-mustaqarra lahā]. Al-Mizan rejects an interpretation limited to the sun’s rotation on its axis, since tajrī implies travel from place to place. Its motion manifests the decree and management of the Mighty, Knowing God, whose acts contain all that is beneficial and cannot be overruled or faulted.
verses.39:
Al-Mizan takes manāzil to mean the moon’s twenty-eight phases in its lunar cycle of roughly twenty-eight days and nights. ʿUrjūn is the yellow, curved stalk of a palm cluster, and qadīm means old; the most apt interpretation is that God ordained the moon’s phases until it returns to a crescent like an old, dry, yellow palm stalk.

The verse concerns the moon as seen by people on earth. It receives sunlight, with about half its sphere illuminated and the other half perpetually dark; as the illuminated portion visible from earth changes, it waxes to fullness and wanes back to its crescent. Its cycle has clear effects on nature, the oceans, and human life.

In light of this earth-centered presentation, Al-Mizan says it is not unreasonable to understand and the sun runs to its own dwelling place (36:38) according to the sun’s perceived daily, seasonal, and yearly movement: it appears to rise and traverse the sky while being, from its own standpoint, essentially at rest relative to the earth. This arrangement is part of the order of earthly life, and God knows best.
verses.40:
Al-Mizan explains lā yanbaghī as meaning that it does not behove or suit the sun to overtake the moon. The cosmos operates continuously and without disorder or violation until its appointed end: the sun and moon have their own paths, and night and day remain sequential, alternating rather than producing two successive nights or days.

The verse mentions the sun rather than the moon overtaking because the sun is stronger, and night rather than day outracing because night is the day’s absence. By denying the stronger’s ability to overtake the weaker, it more forcefully excludes cosmic chaos and also implies that the weaker cannot overtake the stronger.

Falak is the celestial course through which bodies such as the sun, moon, stars, and planets swim. Each may include the sun, moon, night, and day, and the use of plural verbs proper to sentient beings perhaps indicates their willing compliance with the divine will.
verses.41: Al-Mizan presents the carrying of their dhuriyyah in a laden ship as a sign of divine lordship. Dhuriyyah, originally small children, may refer to young and old alike, singly or collectively; al-fulk is a ship and mashḥūn means full. Ocean travel in laden vessels, whether for trade or other purposes, depends on God’s management: only He keeps ships afloat and guards them from sinking, and human use of natural forces remains dependent on Him. Mentioning their descendants rather than themselves is meant to awaken appreciation of divine compassion and mercy.
verses.42: Al-Mizan reports that exegetes commonly understand the similar things people ride to be riding animals. It rejects as unsophisticated the view that the preceding ship was Noah’s ark and that this verse means only later boats, as well as similarly narrow readings such as camels alone. A general interpretation is preferable and may include airplanes and other aerial vessels.
verses.43: Al-Mizan connects this verse to the carrying of their offspring in the laden ark: all such events occur by God’s will. If He willed, He could drown them, leaving them neither ṣarīkh—help in response to their cry—nor rescue from drowning.
verses.44: Al-Mizan explains the exception to mean that no material cause could save them unless God’s mercy reached them, allowing them to continue in enjoyment until their decreed ends.
verses.45:
Al-Mizan says the verse censures those who remain unmoved by the signs proving that God is their Lord. They are called to guard against what is before and behind them; this may mean present and past associationism and disobedience, punishment earned and still to come, or transgression in this world and punishment in the hereafter. The last interpretation is the best.

By leaving unstated what happens when this warning is given, the verse intensifies the portrayal of their audacity and mockery: when called to truth and mindfulness of God, they abandon the caller. Their response is indicated by their turning away from every sign.
verses.46: Al-Mizan holds that the signs from which they turn away include signs they see, verses they hear and contemplate, signs in the natural world and in themselves, and miracles such as the Qur’an. They turn away from them all.
verses.47:
Al-Mizan presents spending on the poor and needy as the compassionate counterpart to worship, the two being the pillars of true religion. The command to spend from what Allah has gifted them establishes that God is the true owner of their wealth. Having created the needy, He has charged those given provision to support them generously rather than miserly.

The explicit labels “those who deny” and “those who believe,” in place of expected pronouns, show that disbelief, turning from truth, and following base desire lead the deniers to make this excuse, while the command comes from believers. Their refusal also rejects the compassion and social reform to which their fiṭrah calls them. They argue that if God willed the needy to have sustenance, He would already have made them rich.

The commentary calls this sophistry, for it confuses divine legislative will (irādah tashrīʿiyyah) with divine creational will (irādah takwīniyyah). The legislative will, which tests people and leads them to happiness in this world and the next, can be disobeyed; the creational will cannot be violated. God legislatively wills those able to share with the less fortunate, but has not coercively imposed this as His creational will, leaving people free to obey or disobey. Thus their claim masks stubborn rebellion against His command, not any failure of His will. Their final charge, “You are clearly astray,” means that they deem believers mistaken for saying God commanded and willed their charity.
verses.48: Al-Mizan explains that the disbelievers mock the warning because they cannot imagine it to be true. Perhaps hādhā (“this”) suggests that the Last Day is near, either in time or in their minds, since the Prophet and believers frequently warned of it. When waʿd is mentioned alone, it includes both bliss and torment; when opposed to waʿīd, waʿd denotes eternal happiness and waʿīd eternal misery.
verses.49: Al-Mizan takes yanẓurūn as awaiting or looking out for, ṣayḥa as the first trumpet blast, and yakhtaṣimūn as arguing or quarrelling. The single cry displays how insignificant their affair is before God: He needs neither effort nor help to destroy them. In answer to their mocking question about the Hour, the verse ironically shows that they await only this sudden blast, from which there will be no escape, while they remain heedlessly occupied in disputes.
verses.50: Al-Mizan explains that the cry brings sudden death. None will have time to make a bequest, nor anyone left to receive one, since all are seized at once; those away from home cannot return to their people.
verses.51: Al-Mizan identifies this as the second trumpet blast, by which the dead are raised. Ajdāth is the plural of jadath, “grave,” and yansilūn means to walk quickly. Their hastening “to their Lord” is reproachful, because those who had disliked divine lordship are now compelled to hasten to their Lord.
verses.52:
Al-Mizan explains baʿathnā as “raised” and marqad as a resting place, here meaning graves. The disbelievers themselves utter the whole statement. Their cry of woe and initial question arise from the heedlessness, denial of resurrection, and absorption in desire that marked their earthly lives. Terrified and bewildered on entering a new world of ruin, they first ask who raised them; then they recall the messengers’ promise of resurrection and requital, implore al-Raḥmān’s mercy despite formerly deriding that name, and confess that the messengers spoke truly.

Some exegetes make “This is what the Merciful promised” a reply by God, angels, or believers to the disbelievers’ question, treating mā in hādhāmā waʿada al-raḥmān in different grammatical ways. Al-Mizan rejects this, especially the verbal-clause reading of mā, because a reply to “Who raised us?” should identify the agent, not merely describe what occurred. The claim that such an answer merely throws their disbelief back at them does not solve the problem. It likewise considers unlikely the view that “this” describes marqadinā—“these, our graves”—and that a new, ellipted sentence means that what the Merciful promised is true. Rather, “This is what the Merciful promised” is a subject-predicate sentence spoken by the disbelievers.
verses.53: Al-Mizan states that the unstated subject means that this event, or this blast, will be only a single cry: it will seize them unexpectedly and gather them without delay or respite. “Before Us” means that all will stand present before God for judgment.
verses.54:
Al-Mizan holds that no soul will be wronged because people are recompensed by their actual deeds. Since injustice is putting a thing in an unsuitable place, burdening one with one’s own deeds is not unjust. The verse’s mode of summoning and addressing people is somewhat metaphorical; it does not establish that these precise words will literally be spoken by God, angels, or believers. Its address includes both the saved and the condemned.

The objection that illā, “except,” excludes believers because God multiplies their rewards is answered by distinguishing actual recompense—deeds for deeds—from additional bounty. A possible alternative is that the righteous will not have reward diminished and the wicked will not have requital intensified, though reward may increase and punishment decrease; on this reading, each is repaid only with the kind of deed performed, good or evil. Al-Mizan objects that this does not resolve the real disagreement about what the verse itself means.
verses.55: Al-Mizan explains shughul as what occupies one and turns attention from all else, and fākihūn as enjoying themselves, taking pleasure, and cheerful bantering. It rejects the view that fākihūn means merely possessing fruit, since fruit is mentioned separately elsewhere. The Garden’s dwellers will be so occupied in its blessings that they will think of nothing else.
verses.56: Al-Mizan explains ẓilāl as shade, whether beneath a roof, portico, tree, or similar shelter, and arāʾik as things upon which one reclines, such as couches or cushions. The dwellers of Paradise will be with their believing wives from earthly life or with the ḥūr al-ʿayn, sheltered in shade and reclining with honor and dignity.
verses.57: Al-Mizan explains fākiha as fruit and yadʿūn as what they wish for. In the Garden, they will have fruit and whatever else their hearts desire.
verses.58: Al-Mizan explains the indefinite “Peace” as an exalted declaration meaning that peace is upon them or belongs to them. Qawlan denotes an utterance. The plain sense is that they receive peace, or a greeting of peace, directly from God, distinct from the greeting of peace offered by the angels.
verses.59: Al-Mizan explains this as God’s command on that day for the guilty to separate from the dwellers of Paradise. It actualizes the distinction between the faithful and righteous on one side, and the corrupt and wicked on the other.
verses.60:
Al-Mizan explains aʿhad as advising or making a bequest. Worshipping Satan means obeying his whispers or directing others to obey him, for obedience belongs to God alone or to those whom God commands people to obey. Satan must not be obeyed because he is an open enemy and an enemy does not approach with goodwill. The interpretation that worshipping Satan means worshipping other deities, called Satan because he embellishes them, is considered contrived.

The guilty are addressed as children of Adam because Satan became Adam’s enemy after refusing God’s command to prostrate to him, being cast out, and becoming hostile to Adam’s descendants. The warning against Satan’s obedience was also conveyed through the messengers and prophets. Some exegetes identify aʿhad with the covenant taken from humanity in the realm of pre-existence, ʿālam al-dharr; Al-Mizan states that this covenant is, in a way, identical with the covenant directed to them in this world.
verses.61: Al-Mizan explains that the command to worship God is joined to, and clarifies, the preceding command not to worship Satan: worship of God is the straight path.
verses.62: Al-Mizan explains jibil as a group, possibly a large group. The question is a gentle reproof for failing to understand how Satan led such a multitude astray.
verses.63: Al-Mizan explains that this is the hell of which prophets and messengers repeatedly warned them, and which God had promised as the destination of the corrupt who follow Iblīs. The wording also implies that hellfire will be roused on that day.
verses.64: Al-Mizan notes that al-ṣalā may mean accompanying and following, from the root w-ṣ-l, while some exegetes take it as enduring heat, from ṣ-l-y. The command is addressed to the disbelievers included among the guilty, because of what they used to reject.
verses.65: Al-Mizan explains that the hands and legs will testify to the deeds for which they were used, each limb speaking concerning sins within its own domain. Hands and feet are examples; other passages also mention the testimony of ears, eyes, hearts, and skin.
verses.66: Al-Mizan explains, citing Majmaʿ al-Bayān, that ṭamasa is eradication that leaves no trace; thus putting out their eyes means completely effacing their sight, so that it cannot return. Though the path itself is clear and does not mislead its traveller, they would be permanently unable to see it and would rush about aimlessly. The view that istabaqū means setting out for the path of truth without being guided to it is unlikely.
verses.67: Al-Mizan, following Majmaʿ al-Bayān, explains maskh as disfigurement or metamorphosis. To transfigure them in their places means that God could transform them where they sit, without their even rising and without means or effort, showing the ease of this for Him. They would then be unable either to move about in their torment or return to their former safe condition; “going” and “coming back” contrast safety with transfiguration and punishment. The interpretation that they could not proceed to their destinations or return to their homes is unlikely.
verses.68: Al-Mizan explains that nuʿammirhu means extending a person's life, while nunakkishu means reversing his constitution: in old age strength becomes weakness, intellect ignorance, and memory forgetfulness. The verse, and perhaps the preceding two as well, shows God returning human beings to an earlier phase of life; He who can do this can also efface their eyes or transfigure them immediately. The closing question rebukes their thoughtlessness and urges reflection.
verses.69: Al-Mizan holds that the verse affirms the truth of the Prophet’s mission and the divine source of his book. Poetry was neither taught to him nor fitting for him, not because of any deficiency or incapacity, but because God raised him above the rank of a bard who fashions illusions and fantasies in pleasing metres. As God’s messenger, whose sign and call are the Qur’an, he cannot properly be called merely a poet. The Qur’an is not poetry at all, but a miraculous divine reminder and clear recitation. The restrictive illā directly refutes those who deny its revelation: dhikr and qurʾān identify it as a reminder recited from the divine precincts.
verses.70: Al-Mizan gives two compatible connections for the verse: it may explain why the Prophet was not taught poetry, so that the accusation of poetry is removed and he can warn those truly alive through the Qur’an; or it may explain why what he recites is only a reminder and clear recitation, sent to warn such people. Thus the purpose of sending both the Messenger and the Qur’an is to warn those who truly live and to establish the word against deniers. “Life” figuratively means employing one’s intellect toward truth and heeding it.
verses.71: Al-Mizan presents livestock as a sign of divine oneness, lordship, and governance of human life. God’s “hand” is metaphorical: it signifies that creation belongs exclusively to Him and therefore excludes partners in His creative act. Since livestock were created for human beings, their exclusive use entails ownership or control, as ordinary social ownership arises from exclusivity of use. There is no need to posit an omitted phrase to connect their creation for people with their control over them; the two statements follow naturally. Nor should mālikūn mean merely power or subjugation, for that would make the following verse’s distinct statement that the animals were subjected to people a mere repetition.
verses.72: Al-Mizan explains that dhalalnāhum means that livestock were made docile and compliant, enabling human control. Rakūb denotes beasts of burden, such as camels and cows, upon which loads are carried; the others are eaten for their meat.
verses.73: Al-Mizan explains that livestock provide further benefits, including wool, hair, hides, and milk; mashārib, literally “drinks,” here means milk. Taken together, the verses say that God created livestock for human beings as part of His governance of worldly life, gave people unopposed control over them, made them docile, and enabled people to use some for carrying loads and others for food. Their other products and milk likewise benefit people. The call to gratitude asks whether they will recognize this perfect ordering as evidence of God’s lordship and worship Him thankfully for His blessings.
verses.74: Al-Mizan explains that “they” are the polytheists, and their gods are idols, lesser demons (shayāṭīn), or Pharaoh-like men who deify themselves, rather than angels near to God or human saints, who do not fit the description in the following verse. They sought these beings’ help because they believed them delegated by God to manage the universe in beneficial and harmful matters. They therefore worshipped them to placate them, hoping to retain their blessings and avoid their wrath.
verses.75: Al-Mizan states that the gods adopted by the polytheists cannot help them, since they possess no power for good or harm. The most fitting reading of “they will be a host brought before them” takes the first pronoun as the polytheists and the second as their deities: the polytheists are the gods’ soldiery, and soldiery entails obedience, so the worshippers obey their gods rather than the reverse. Muḥḍarūn means being brought for reckoning on the Day of Resurrection. Hence these impotent demigods will be brought forward with their obedient followers. The alternatives that the worshippers are their gods’ earthly fighters, that the gods are a force prepared to punish the worshippers, or that they attend merely to witness punishment or destroy hope of intercession are to be rejected.
verses.76: Al-Mizan explains that the opening “so” follows from the preceding exposure of idolatry: those from whom the polytheists seek aid cannot help them and will instead be brought forward for punishment. The Prophet therefore should not grieve over their idolatrous speech. God is neither heedless nor unable to respond, for He knows both the sentiments they conceal and what they openly declare.
verses.77: Al-Mizan treats the verse as part of the argument for resurrection, and possibly as an elaboration of the hostile speech alluded to previously. “Seeing” means certain knowledge: human beings know that God created them from a lowly, indefinite “droplet,” yet become khaṣīm, openly quarrelsome adversaries of their Creator. The interrogative form expresses astonishment at one who knows this origin but nevertheless turns into an evident enemy.
verses.78: Al-Mizan explains ramīm as decomposed. The question, “Who will resurrect these bones when they have rotted?” spells out the likeness or analogy that the denier has made against God. In making it, he forgets that he himself was first created from a mere droplet. Reflection on his original creation would refute his own objection to resurrection; accordingly, God directs this answer to the Prophet.
verses.79: Al-Mizan explains that the Prophet is instructed to answer that the One who first brought the bones into existence, anshaʾaha, will give them life again. God knows every aspect of His creations: He neither forgets nor is ignorant of what happens to these bones before and after death. Thus no unawareness or forgetfulness can prevent Him from reviving them.
verses.80: Al-Mizan explains tūqidūn as lighting a fire. The verse further clarifies God’s power to originate creation by refuting the claim that life cannot return to what is lifeless. God makes a green, dewy tree a source of fire: exegetes identify it as shajara al-markh and shajara al-ʿafār, whose green branches are struck together to kindle fire by God’s permission. Restoring life to the dead is no more astonishing than drawing fire from a green tree, since both unite apparent opposites.
verses.81:
Al-Mizan reads the rhetorical question as an argument for resurrection from the greater creation of the heavens and earth: the Creator of that vast, ordered realm cannot be unable to revive human beings, who are only a small part of it. “Something similar” (bi-mithlihim) means creating their likeness. It cannot simply mean “themselves,” since the context concerns resurrection rather than a repeated creation of the heavens and earth; nor does the pronoun refer to the heavens and earth and everything within them, because the question concerns resurrecting humans and expressly says creating their like.

The commentary concludes, following al-Ṭabrisī in Majmaʿ al-Bayān, that creating their likeness means returning people to life for recompense after death. Human personality is preserved by the independent, immaterial soul, not by a body whose parts continually change and decay. The soul therefore does not perish with the body but returns to God. In the afterlife the body appears as a likeness of the former body, yet the person is identical with the former person because the soul is the same. The deniers question the creation of new bodies, not souls; God accordingly affirms the possibility of recreating bodies like their former ones. This does not negate their return as the same people: their preserved souls are reattached to their recreated bodies, and the dead are revived exactly as they were in this life.
verses.82:
Al-Mizan explains that the verse declares God’s absolute independence in bringing whatever He wills into being: nothing besides His exalted essence is needed either to produce or prevent existence. Although related verses call this “Our word,” amr here means “matter,” not a verbal command; the point is the ease of creation, not the particular word by which God creates. “Whenever He wills something” means whenever He wills its coming into existence. Qaḍā may likewise denote divine decree and will, while creational will means placing the object under a will from which it has no escape.

“He says to it ‘Be!’” cannot be a physical utterance. A literal voice would require another creative word to produce the apparatus for that first speech, producing infinite regress; moreover, a thing not yet created cannot possess ears by which to hear. The expression is therefore metaphorical: creation proceeds immediately from God’s essence, with neither intermediary nor delay. The view, common among many early exegetes, that “Be!” is an actual spoken word is untenable. Nor is it valid to abandon such rational examination on the ground that God transcends the intellect, for intellectual proof underlies religious knowledge, including proof of the divine Book’s unblemished character.

During creation there is only God and the created object, with no third party between them. Divine will, though an attribute of act, may be regarded as a cause distinct from the divine essence only after the object exists; it is above being an actual action, lest things cease to need God for their existence. Nor is there an entity other than God called “existence” or “bringing into existence” that mediates a thing’s existence. Creation is solely the relation between God and the thing.

Thus the creational “Be!” is the created thing’s very existence insofar as that existence is linked to and dependent on God. Considered as a distinct thing, it is a being (mawjūd), not something in the process of being brought into being (ījād), and a created thing (makhlūq), not creation (khalq). What God bestows in this respect has no pause, lapse, change, variation, or stages; any such features visible in creation belong to created things, not to their relation to their Lord. “And it is” shows the created thing’s immediate obedience to the divine command through being.
verses.83: Al-Mizan explains malakūt as an intensified form of mulk, meaning ownership or dominion. In light of the preceding verse, malakūt concerns the aspect of things facing God, whereas mulk concerns their aspect facing creation, or both aspects together. Saying that this dominion is in God’s hands emphasizes His exclusive authority over all things, in which no other has a share. The verse answers polytheists who doubt resurrection because they neglect this universal divine authority: God is exalted above their objections. The return to Him addresses all people, believers and unbelievers alike, and concludes the discussion.
